scenes_rel.name: Nueva psicodelia y big music: Echo & the Bunnymen y U2

podcast.title: Acquisition by Zamba
podcast.body: In the spring of 1998, Zoo was acquired by Zamba, at which point Zoo's name was changed to Volcano. This acquisition and subsequent renaming marked another shift in the complex corporate ownership Tool faced. "In the spring of 1998, Zoo was bought by Zamba, whereupon Zoo's name was changed to Volcano."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Confusing Name Changes
podcast.body: After being absorbed into Volcano, the entity underwent confusing name changes, including Volcano changing to Free World, then Free World Entertainment changing back to Zoo Entertainment, and then simply Zoo. These changes caused significant confusion and paralysis for Tool. "And then just for kicks, Free World Entertainment changed its name back to Zoo Entertainment, and then just back to Zoo."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Affiliation and Artist Roster
podcast.body: Zoo Entertainment was the label Tool initially chose, affiliated at the time with BMG, which was a standalone major label. It also served as the label for Green Jelly, providing a level of comfort for Tool's drummer Danny Carey, who had played with Green Jelly. "Tool decided to go with a label called Zoo Entertainment."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Financial Troubles & Acquisitions
podcast.body: By April 1993, when Tool's debut album *Undertow* was released, Zoo was already experiencing financial trouble. In 1995, its parent label BMG laid off numerous staff, leading to Zoo's sale to Volcano Entertainment in 1996. For a period, Zoo and Volcano co-existed as a partnership, with Zoo retaining custody of Tool's second album, *Anima*. "Zoo was in financial trouble."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Founded by Bill Drummond
podcast.body: Zoo Records was a label founded by Bill Drummond, who would later achieve fame as a co-founder of The KLF. "Drummond used to be the manager of Echo and the Bunnyman in the early days, and was the founder of a label called Zoo Records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Royalty & Contract Disputes
podcast.body: Zoo was criticized for being "really slow with the royalty checks" for the briskly selling *Anima* album, and the initial payment was significantly smaller than expected. Critically, Zoo (then absorbed into Volcano) "forgot to pick up the option" for Tool's contract renewal. This oversight, attributed to the formality falling through the cracks, led to Tool deciding they no longer wished to deal with the company, which in turn prompted Zoo to sue Tool for breach of contract. "Then, Tool found out that Zoo, Volcano, forgot, forgot to pick up the option for Tools Contract."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
